  \item \textbf{Evaluation set}: 5{,}000 held-out sequences for perplexity measurement.

\end{itemize}

\subsection{Recursive Training Protocol}

Generation~0 is the pretrained checkpoint with no additional fine-tuning.
For each subsequent generation $t = 1, \ldots, T$ with $T{=}10$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]

  \item \textbf{Checkpoint and evaluate.} Save $M_t$; measure all metrics on held-out data.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Models and Datasets}

We use \textbf{Pythia-410M-deduped}~\cite{biderman2023pythia} (405M parameters, $D{=}1024$) as the primary model and \textbf{Pythia-1B-deduped} (1042M parameters, $D{=}2048$) for scale-transfer validation.
Both are decoder-only transformers pretrained on the deduplicated Pile~\cite{gao2020pile}.

From the Pile (uncopyrighted split, \texttt{monology/pile-uncopyrighted}), we sample three disjoint subsets:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Training pool}: 50{,}000 sequences of 512 tokens for fine-tuning.
  \item \textbf{Evaluation set}: 5{,}000 held-out sequences for perplexity measurement.
  \item \textbf{Spectral probe set}: 1{,}000 held-out sequences for effective rank computation.
\end{itemize}
All sequences are tokenized with the GPTNeoX tokenizer (vocabulary size 50{,}304) and truncated or padded to 512 tokens.
We retain only sequences with at least 256 non-padding tokens ($\geq$50\% fill ratio) to ensure sufficient context for representation extraction.

\subsection{Recursive Training Protocol}

Generation~0 is the pretrained checkpoint with no additional fine-tuning.
For each subsequent generation $t = 1, \ldots, T$ with $T{=}10$:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Synthetic generation.} Sample 50{,}000 sequences from $M_{t-1}$ via ancestral sampling (temperature $= 1.0$, top-$k = 50$, no nucleus filtering, max length 512 tokens, batch size 32).
  \item \textbf{Data mixing.} Combine synthetic samples with real data at condition-specific ratio $r_t$ (see \S\ref{sec:conditions}).  The number of real samples mixed in is $\lfloor n_{\text{syn}} \cdot r_t / (1 - r_t) \rfloor$, drawn uniformly without replacement from the training pool.
  \item \textbf{Fine-tuning.} Train $M_{t-1}$ for 1 epoch on the mixed corpus $\rightarrow M_t$.
  \item \textbf{Checkpoint and evaluate.} Save $M_t$; measure all metrics on held-out data.
\end{enumerate}

Training hyperparameters are fixed across all conditions: AdamW optimizer with learning rate $5{\times}10^{-5}$, weight decay $0.01$, batch size~8 with gradient accumulation~4 (effective batch size~32), linear warmup over 5\% of steps followed by linear decay, and gradient clipping at $\|\mathbf{g}\|_{\max} = 1.0$.
The number of optimizer steps per generation varies with the mixing ratio: ${\sim}1{,}562$ steps for pure synthetic ($r_t = 0$) to ${\sim}3{,}125$ steps at $r_t = 0.50$.

\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}

\paragraph{Effective Rank (RankMe).}
Following \citet{rankme2023}, we forward-pass the 1{,}000 spectral probe samples through $M_t$, extract last-layer hidden states, mean-pool across sequence length to obtain $\mathbf{Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{1000 \times D}$, compute its SVD, and report
\begin{equation}
  \rho(\mathbf{Z}) = \exp\!\Bigl(-\sum_i p_i \log p_i\Bigr), \quad p_i = \frac{\sigma_i}{\sum_j \sigma_j},
\end{equation}
where $\sigma_i$ are the singular values of $\mathbf{Z}$.
Lower effective rank signals representation collapse.
We measure spectral decline relative to Generation~1 (post-adaptation baseline) rather than Generation~0 (pretrained), as the pretrained-to-fine-tuned transition induces a shift in representation anisotropy unrelated to recursive collapse.
We use RankMe rather than SIGMA's Track~I bound~\cite{sigma2026} because (a)~no public implementation of SIGMA exists as of May 2026, (b)~RankMe is architecture-agnostic and hyperparameter-free, and (c)~RankMe's spectral entropy formulation provides a smooth, monotonic collapse indicator suitable for closed-loop control.

\paragraph{Spectral Log-Volume.}
From the same SVD decomposition, we compute
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{Z}) = \sum_{i:\,\sigma_i > \epsilon} \log \sigma_i, \quad \epsilon = 10^{-10},
\end{equation}
which equals $\tfrac{1}{2}\log\det(\mathbf{Z}^\top\mathbf{Z})$ up to the threshold $\epsilon$.
This captures the overall representational volume on a logarithmic scale and is more sensitive to the tail of the singular spectrum

\subsection{Statistical Design}

Each condition is run with 3 random seeds (42, 123, 7), paired across conditions (i.e., all four conditions share the same seed set) to reduce variance from initialization and data ordering.

  \item Monotonically decreasing effective rank across Generations~1--10 (allowing at most one non-monotone generation).

  \item Closed-loop (adaptive) vs.\ open-loop (linear-increasing): $\geq$1.5 perplexity point improvement.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Compute budget.}
The full experiment comprises 1 Phase~0 pilot chain (single seed, 10 generations) and 12 Phase~1 chains (4 conditions $\times$ 3 seeds $\times$ 10 generations), totaling 130 generation-steps.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   I am the independent Research Reviewer (Loop #5, continued from context compaction) for the `spectral_collapse_ews` project. My role is to independently verify experiment conclusions, audit GPU resource usage, check data integrity, review paper sections from an adversarial reviewer perspective, and report findings to Director via `reviewer_post_to_director`. I operate read-only. The project studies spectral collapse in recursive synthetic training of LLMs, using embedding Gram matrix spectral log-volume (SLV) as an early warning signal. The paper targets EMNLP 2026 ARR Short Paper, May 25 deadline (~7 days away).

   Key hard constraints from handoff:
   - GPU whitelist: cuda:0 and cuda:1 only (rtx6000-diagprobe, 2× RTX PRO 6000, 98GB each)
   - exp_005 (PID 116947) runs via nohup — never restart without checking /proc first
   - D015: Paper main parameter is k=10 (not k=20); exp_005 (k=20) is sensitivity data only
   - D004: Collapse measured from Gen 1 baseline (Gen 0→1 rise is pretrained decompression)
   - Root partition only 5.2G free (83%) — exp_002 died from this before

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Recursive synthetic training: training LLMs on their own generated output across multiple generations
   - Spectral collapse: monotonic decline of effective rank and log_det of embedding Gram matrix over generations
   - Spectral Log-Volume (SLV): S_t = Σ log σ_i — the core EWS metric
   - Decompression phase: initial Gen 0-2 increase in spectral metrics before collapse onset
   - SpectralController (controller.py): budget-constrained proportional controller using formula r_{t+1} = B_rem/(T-t) + k·max(0, Δ_t - τ)
   - per_gen signal mode: delta = (S̃_prev - S̃_current)/|S̃_0| with EMA smoothing (alpha=0.5)
   - Signal attenuation paradox: mixing real data reduces collapse signal, creating self-stabilizing negative feedback
   - Phase 0: pure synthetic (100% synthetic) — baseline collapse characterization (exp_001, DONE, Gen 0-10)
   - Phase 1: four conditions comparison — pure_collapse, fixed_mix (50/50), linear_increasing, adaptive (spectral-guided)
   - Paper framing (D013): main contribution = spectral EWS detection + collapse characterization; controller = proof-of-concept
   - PYTHONUNBUFFERED issue: exp_005 lacks this env var, causing stdout buffering in nohup mode

     - Path format includes k for adaptive: `{condition}_k{k}_seed{seed}`

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Introduction}

Training language models on their own synthetic outputs across multiple generations leads to \emph{model collapse}, a progressive narrowing of the learned distribution that degrades generation quality~\cite{shumailov2024}.
Recent empirical and theoretical work reveals that this degradation is not linear: spectral contraction in representation spaces accelerates around generation 20~\cite{sigma2026}, tail distributions compound with each generation~\cite{shumailov2024}, and degradation rates double past inflection points in the synthetic proportion~\cite{calibration2025}.
This non-linear acceleration makes the \emph{timing} of corrective intervention as important as its magnitude.

The dominant mitigation strategy is mixing real data into the synthetic training pipeline.
Theoretical analyses identify optimal static mixing ratios, notably the golden ratio $\phi^{-1} \approx 0.618$~\cite{he2025golden}, and data accumulation strategies that prevent collapse in principle~\cite{gerstgrasser2024, garg2025}.
However, static ratios assume constant collapse pressure across generations, an assumption contradicted by the empirical evidence of non-linear acceleration.
Meanwhile, spectral monitoring tools like SIGMA~\cite{sigma2026} diagnose collapse in rich detail but prescribe no intervention.
Adaptive sampling methods such as DCES~\cite{dces2026} redistribute \emph{within} the synthetic pool but do not control the global real-to-synthetic ratio.
No existing system closes the feedback loop from spectral diagnosis to adaptive real-data allocation.

We present, to our knowledge, the first closed-loop system connecting spectral collapse monitoring to budget-constrained adaptive mixing.
Our key insight is that a fixed real-data budget achieves improved collapse prevention when allocated \emph{temporally}, with real data concentrated at generations of peak collapse pressure rather than spread uniformly.
We monitor representational health via effective rank~\cite{rankme2023} and spectral log-volume of output embeddings, and feed the spectral log-volume signal into a proportional controller that adjusts the real-data fraction generation-by-generation while guaranteeing total budget adherence.
The design is budget-fixed by construction: our method and the uniform baseline consume identical amounts of real data, isolating the effect of temporal allocation.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
\item We provide the first spectral-level characterization of recursive synthetic training collapse and identify three distinct phases through joint tracking of effective rank, spectral log-volume, perplexity, and HellaSwag accuracy (Section~\ref{sec:spectral_trajectory}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0_metrics}).
\item We show that spectral log-volume serves as an early warning signal (EWS) for collapse: it declines before effective rank and exhibits greater temporal lead in larger models (Section~\ref{sec:cross_validation}).
\item We introduce a budget-constrained proportional controller driven by spectral log-volume decline rate that reallocates a fixed real-data budget temporally, and validate improved perplexity and downstream accuracy over uniform and scheduled baselines (Section~\ref{sec:controller}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0_metrics}).
\end{itemize}

Our experiments on Pythia-410M across 10 recursive generations show that spectral-guided adaptive allocation achieves [X] lower perplexity and [Y\%] higher HellaSwag accuracy compared to uniform allocation with identical total real-data consumption.
In addition to fixed uniform and spectral-guided adaptive conditions, we include open-loop heuristic schedules (e.g., linear-increasing allocation) to isolate the incremental value of closed-loop feedback.
These results establish that \emph{when} real data is introduced matters, not just \emph{how much}. This finding supports the case for closed-loop intervention in synthetic training pipelines.

{"success": true, "data": {"stdout": "\section{Conclusion}

We presented the first spectral-level characterization of embedding representation evolution during recursive synthetic training. Joint tracking of effective rank, spectral log-volume (SLV), perplexity, and HellaSwag accuracy across 10 generations of Pythia-410M reveals three distinct phases: pretrained anisotropy decompression in Generation 1, a decompression peak at Generation 2, and sustained collapse decline from Generation 3 onward. These phases are consistent across metrics but differ in timing and sensitivity, which motivates careful signal selection for early intervention. The four-indicator framework provides a multi-resolution view of representational health that no single metric captures alone.

Our central finding is that spectral log-volume functions as a more sensitive early warning signal for collapse than effective rank. In Pythia-410M experiments, SLV onset signal strength exceeds that of effective rank by a factor of 6.7$\times$. Cross-validation on Pythia-1B demonstrates at least one generation of temporal lead: SLV begins its decline at Generation 2 while effective rank continues to rise. This temporal advantage is critical for closed-loop systems, where earlier detection translates directly into earlier corrective action. Spectral log-volume thus provides the earliest actionable signal for collapse onset among the indicators we evaluated.

We introduced a budget-constrained proportional controller that uses SLV decline rate to drive adaptive real-data mixing decisions. The controller reallocates a fixed real-data budget across generations, with real data concentrated at generations of peak collapse pressure rather than spread uniformly. By construction, total real-data consumption remains identical to the uniform baseline; this design isolates the effect of temporal redistribution. \textbf{[TBD: Phase 1 results]} Future work includes cross-architecture validation on additional model families, extension to larger parameter counts, and evaluation under RLHF and DPO alignment pipelines where synthetic data is pervasive.

\subsection{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
  \item Validated on a single model family (Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}); generalization to other architectures remains unverified.
  \item Fixed data scale (50K samples per generation from The Pile~\cite{gao2020pile}).
  \item Controller hyperparameters ($\tau$, $k$) require offline calibration from a Phase~0 pilot run.
  \item Evaluated on a single text domain; multi-domain robustness is untested.
  \item Phase~0 go/no-go judgment is based on a single seed (\texttt{seed=42}); Phase~1 introduces 3-seed statistical testing.
  \item Any 1B scale-transfer results are from a single-seed pilot only.
\end{itemize}
